newsitem.title: USA: Man guilty of killing fellow talk show guest.
newsitem.headline: Man guilty of killing fellow talk show guest.

text.p: A jury on Tuesday found a television talk show guest guilty of second-degree murder for killing another man who revealed a crush on him during the taping of the show.
Jonathan Schmitz, 26, blinked as the verdict was read but showed little emotion as he was led away in handcuffs. Sentencing was scheduled for Dec. 4.
Schmitz admitted shooting Scott Amedure, 32, on March 9, 1995, three days after Amedure revealed during a taping of the "Jenny Jones" talk show that he had a crush on Schmitz.

The show was never aired, but it was replayed for the jurors and portions of it were repeated on television newscasts. In it Schmitz appeared surprised but not overly chagrined when Amedure, an acquaintance and neighbour, revealed himelf as his admirer.
Schmitz, seen laughing and then burying his face in his hands, told the studio audience he was not gay.

The second degree murder conviction carries a penalty under Michigan law of life in prison but with the possibility of parole. Had the jury found him guilty as charged of premeditated first-degree murder state law would have mandated a life sentence without parole.
Testimony during the trial revealed Amedure sent a suggestive note to Schmitz after the two had returned home. Schmitz admitted he shot Amedure, after which he surrendered to police.
Attorneys for Schmitz said the humiliation he suffered from the show, coupled with mental illnesses at the time of the shooting, prevented him from being able to form an intent to murder.
Jones, whose Chicago-based programme has a wide following, testified during the trial, denying that the show, which featured cases of same-sex secret admirers, was a case of "ambush television."
During a subsequent show Jones read an apology to the parties involved in the killing.
Schmitz's father, Allyn, testified his son had a history of alcohol abuse and suicide attempts but that before going on the TV show he had turned his life around with a new job.

Schmitz was excited about going on the show, his father said, and speculated on which woman, but never any man, might be his secret admirer. He said before the show was taped he would be "knee deep" in women after it aired, his father said.
Producers testified during the trial that Schmitz was told his secret admirer could be either a man or a woman.
